name: Emerging Trust Tech
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: After Blockchain: The Next Wave of Trust Infrastructure
lesson.summary: Blockchain is one point in a broader family of trust technologies, verifiable credentials, standalone zero-knowledge proofs, trusted execution environments, and DAG-based ledgers among them, each at a different, honestly assessable stage of maturity.
lesson.body:
This course has treated blockchain as a specific answer to a general problem: how do independent parties who don't fully trust each other agree on facts, verify claims, or coordinate without a single controlling intermediary. It is worth stepping back, in this next-to-last chapter of the course, to see blockchain as one member of a larger family of trust technologies rather than the final word on the problem, especially since several of blockchain's individual components have already spun off into standalone tools that don't require a full chain at all.

Verifiable credentials and decentralized identifiers, standardized by the W3C, let an issuer, say a university, cryptographically sign a claim, such as a degree, that a holder can present to any verifier without the verifier needing to contact the university directly, and without necessarily requiring a blockchain at all; some implementations anchor a small amount of state to a ledger for revocation checking, but the core credential exchange is a cryptographic protocol, not a chain. Zero-knowledge proofs, introduced earlier in this course as a privacy tool used inside certain blockchains, are increasingly deployed as standalone infrastructure: a system can let a user prove a fact, that they are over eighteen, that their income exceeds a threshold, that a computation was performed correctly, without revealing the underlying data, entirely outside any ledger. Trusted execution environments, hardware-based secure enclaves built into modern processors, offer a different trust model entirely: instead of many parties reaching consensus, a single tamper-resistant chip attests that code ran unmodified and data stayed confidential, a model sometimes combined with blockchains and sometimes used to replace them for confidential computing tasks.

Directed acyclic graph ledgers, used by projects such as Hedera Hashgraph and IOTA, keep the goal of a shared, tamper-evident record of transactions but abandon the strictly linear chain-of-blocks structure this course has spent so much time on, aiming for higher throughput or lower fees by letting transactions reference multiple prior transactions in a graph rather than a single chain. Whether that structural difference amounts to a genuinely distinct trust model or a variation on the same underlying idea is itself a useful question to practice the evidence-based evaluation habits from earlier in this course on, rather than accepting either a vendor's or a skeptic's framing at face value.

Applying technology readiness level honestly across this landscape is instructive precisely because these technologies are not uniformly mature. Trusted execution environments are shipped in billions of consumer devices today and sit close to TRL 9 as a general hardware capability, even though specific confidential-computing applications built on top of them may be much earlier. Verifiable credentials have real, if still limited, production deployments in areas like digital identity wallets and are best placed in the TRL 6 to 8 range depending on the specific use case. Some proposed DAG-based consensus mechanisms and newer zero-knowledge proof systems remain closer to TRL 3 or 4, promising in research and early demonstration but not yet proven at the scale their advocates project. The discipline this course has built, asking what problem a technology actually solves, where it sits on the hype cycle, and what TRL it has honestly earned, applies just as well to whatever comes after blockchain as it did to blockchain itself, which is the real point of teaching it.
